title: Sunrise Arc (NIRCam Image)
caption: The galaxy cluster WHL0137-08 and the Sunrise Arc, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: WHL-J24.3324-8.477, Earendel · constellation Cetus · about 12.9 billion light-years away (source figure)
credit: Image: NASA, ESA, CSA; Science: Dan Coe (STScI/AURA for ESA, JHU), Brian Welch (NASA-GSFC, UMD); Image Processing: Zoltan Levay

recognition.text: NASA Webb image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Fuzzy white galaxies gather at the center of this Webb view, surrounded by redder, curved galaxies much farther away. The white ones belong to the massive galaxy cluster WHL0137-08. Just below the diffraction spike at the 5 o'clock position lies a red smear, the Sunrise Arc, the most strongly magnified galaxy known from the universe's first billion years.

Inside the arc sits Earendel, about 12.9 billion light-years away and the most distant star ever detected, seen as it was about 1 billion years after the big bang. The cluster's mass warps space into a natural magnifying glass, and Earendel lies along a wrinkle of maximum magnification that boosts it by a factor of at least 4,000. Hubble discovered the star, and Webb's Near-Infrared Camera then revealed a massive B-type star with over twice the Sun's temperature and about a million times more luminous.
Astronomers think its colors hint at a cooler, redder companion. As the universe expanded, that light was stretched past the wavelengths Hubble can detect, so only Webb could pick it up.

understand.summary: Webb's Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) took the image, with F090W, F115W and F150W shown in blue, F200W in cyan, F277W in green, F356W in yellow, F410M in orange and F444W in red.
understand.eye: All of these filters record infrared light that the eye cannot see, and the colors translate those wavelengths into visible hues.

explore: The arc also contains young star-forming regions and older star clusters as small as 10 light-years across, mirrored on either side of the line of greatest magnification. Two small dots beside Earendel are images of a single cluster, thought to be no younger than 10 million years and probably bound tightly enough to survive to the present day, a hint of how the Milky Way's globular clusters might have looked when they formed.
sources: NASA release: Webb Reveals Colors of Earendel, Most Distant Star Ever Detected
